c.periodos.ubaid.descripcion: First villages and mud-brick temples in southern Mesopotamia, such as Eridu. The dates are approximate and vary by region.
c.periodos.uruk.descripcion: The first cities emerge, led by Uruk. Toward the end come the first administrative tablets, in proto-cuneiform, and the cylinder seal.
c.periodos.dinastico-arcaico.descripcion: The Sumerian city-states (Ur, Lagash, Kish, Uruk, Umma) compete with one another. The first literary texts are written, at Fara and Abu Salabikh.
c.periodos.acadio.descripcion: Sargon of Akkad and his successors unify Mesopotamia for the first time. Akkadian becomes the language of administration. Dates follow the Middle Chronology and are approximate.
c.periodos.ur-iii.descripcion: The last centralized Sumerian-speaking state. Ur-Nammu and Shulgi build ziggurats and promote Sumerian literature.
c.periodos.paleobabilonico.descripcion: The dynasties of Isin, Larsa and Babylon, with Hammurabi as the central figure. Scribes copy most of the Sumerian literature we know and compose major works in Akkadian.
c.periodos.casita-mesoasirio.descripcion: The Kassites rule Babylon while Assyria becomes a major power. Literary texts are fixed in canonical versions, in Standard Babylonian. Approximate boundaries.
c.periodos.neoasirio.descripcion: Assyria dominates the Near East from Kalhu (Nimrud), Dur-Sharrukin and Nineveh. Ashurbanipal assembles his great library in the 7th century BC.
c.periodos.neobabilonico.descripcion: Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II rebuild Babylon, its ziggurat Etemenanki and Marduk's Esagila temple.
c.periodos.aquemenida.descripcion: Cyrus the Great conquers Babylon and brings it into the Persian Empire. The temples and Babylonian astronomy remain active.
c.periodos.seleucida.descripcion: After Alexander the Great, the temples of Babylon and Uruk keep cuneiform writing alive. Berossus writes his history of Babylon in Greek, and mathematical astronomy flourishes.
c.entradas.enuma-elish.fecha_texto: Date of composition debated: most place it around 1100 BC, under Nebuchadnezzar I; Lambert (2013) puts it between that reign and c. 900 BC. The oldest copies, from Assur, date to the 9th century BC.
c.entradas.enuma-elish.resumen: An Akkadian poem on seven tablets. It tells how the gods arise from the mingling of the fresh waters (Apsu) and the salt waters (Tiamat), and how the young god Marduk defeats Tiamat and forms heaven and earth from her body. Thanks to this victory he becomes king of the gods.
c.entradas.enuma-elish.interpretacion:
For Assyriology, the Enuma Elish is not a universal creation story but a theological and political work. Its purpose is to justify placing Marduk, god of the city of Babylon, at the head of the pantheon, a position previously held by Enlil of Nippur. Many scholars connect its composition with the return of Marduk's statue from Elam under Nebuchadnezzar I (c. 1125–1104 BC), although the date is still disputed. The poem reworks older motifs, such as Ninurta's battle against Anzu, and ends with a long exaltation of Marduk's fifty names.

Late ritual texts indicate that it was recited in Babylon during the New Year festival (akitu), in the month of Nisannu. In Assyria, versions circulated in which Ashur replaces Marduk, showing that the text was adapted for political ends. The old idea that Tiamat is an echo of the biblical tehom (the 'deep') or a direct reflection of Genesis is now qualified: parallels in vocabulary and motifs are accepted, but not simple dependence.
c.entradas.enuma-elish.detalles.0: It fills seven tablets and about 1,100 lines.
c.entradas.enuma-elish.detalles.1: Ea (Enki) kills Apsu and builds his dwelling on top of him. Marduk is born there.
c.entradas.enuma-elish.detalles.2: Tiamat creates eleven monsters and names Qingu leader of her army, giving him the Tablet of Destinies.
c.entradas.enuma-elish.detalles.3: Marduk splits Tiamat in two like a dried fish: with one half he makes the sky and with the other the earth. From Qingu's blood, Ea creates humankind to work in place of the gods.
c.entradas.enuma-elish.detalles.4: The gods build the Esagila temple in Babylon for Marduk. Tablet VII lists his fifty names, among them Nēberu.
c.entradas.enuma-elish.detalles.5: The first tablets to be published came from the Library of Ashurbanipal and were made known by George Smith in 1876.
c.entradas.enuma-elish.fuentes_primarias: Tablets from Assur (9th century BC onward)
Copies from Kish, Sultantepe, Babylon, Uruk and Sippar
c.entradas.gilgamesh.nombre_original: ša naqba īmuru (Akkadian, 'He who saw the deep'); old version: šūtur eli šarrī ('Surpassing all kings'); in Sumerian, Bilgames
c.entradas.gilgamesh.fecha_texto: The Sumerian poems are known from Old Babylonian copies (c. 1800 BC), and some perhaps go back to Ur III. The Old Babylonian version dates to c. 1800–1700 BC. The Standard version, attributed to Sîn-lēqi-unninni, is dated c. 1200–1100 BC (debated).
c.entradas.gilgamesh.resumen: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, treats his people harshly until the gods create Enkidu, who becomes his friend. Together they kill Huwawa and the Bull of Heaven. When Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh seeks immortality from Utnapishtim, the survivor of the flood, and fails.
c.entradas.gilgamesh.interpretacion:
Andrew George describes the epic as a meditation on death, friendship and the limits of being human. The Standard version emphasizes the wisdom aspect: Gilgamesh returns to Uruk and finds consolation in the walls of his city, a lasting human achievement. The text grew in layers. First there were independent Sumerian poems about Bilgames; then, around the Old Babylonian period, an Akkadian epic; and finally the Standard version on twelve tablets. Tablet XII translates the second half of the Sumerian poem 'Bilgames, Enkidu and the Netherworld' almost literally and fits poorly with the preceding narrative.

Gilgamesh may have been a historical Early Dynastic king of Uruk (c. 2700 BC), but there are no inscriptions of his, so his historicity is unconfirmed. The flood story in Tablet XI comes from the Atrahasis tradition. When George Smith identified it in 1872, it made a great impact because of its parallels with Genesis.
c.entradas.gilgamesh.detalles.0: The Standard version fills twelve tablets, and tradition attributes it to the scholar Sîn-lēqi-unninni.
c.entradas.gilgamesh.detalles.1: Tablet XI tells of the flood in Utnapishtim's words, with the boat, the birds sent out and the final sacrifice.
c.entradas.gilgamesh.detalles.2: George Smith recognized the flood story on tablet K 3375 in the British Museum in 1872.
c.entradas.gilgamesh.detalles.3: There are five Sumerian poems about Bilgames, among them 'Bilgames and Huwawa' and 'Bilgames and the Bull of Heaven' (ETCSL 1.8.1).
c.entradas.gilgamesh.detalles.4: Fragments have been found outside Mesopotamia: at Hattusa, Megiddo, Emar and Ugarit.
c.entradas.gilgamesh.fuentes_primarias.1: Old Babylonian tablets (Pennsylvania tablet and Yale tablet)
c.entradas.gilgamesh.fuentes_primarias.2: Fragments from Hattusa, Megiddo, Emar and Ugarit
c.entradas.gilgamesh.fuentes_primarias.3: Tablets from Nippur and Ur (Sumerian poems)
c.entradas.atrahasis.nombre_original: inūma ilū awīlum (Akkadian, 'When the gods were like men'); Atra-ḫasīs = 'the exceedingly wise'
c.entradas.atrahasis.fecha_texto: The most complete copy was made by the scribe Ipiq-Aya under Ammi-saduqa of Babylon, c. 1646–1626 BC (Middle Chronology). There are later Neo-Assyrian recensions.
c.entradas.atrahasis.resumen: The lesser gods (Igigi), tired of digging the canals for the great gods, rebel. To replace them, Enki and the mother goddess create human beings from clay and the blood of a slain god. When humankind multiplies and makes too much noise, Enlil sends plagues and, finally, a flood. Atrahasis survives because Enki warns him.
c.entradas.atrahasis.interpretacion:
The poem explains why humankind exists: to serve the gods by working the land and offering them sacrifices. It also explains why humans are mortal and have demographic limits. At the end of the poem, mechanisms of population control are established, such as infant mortality and priestesses who must not bear children. Scholars debate whether the 'noise' (rigmu) of humans is a problem of overpopulation, of rebellion or of disorder in general.

It is the main source for the flood in Gilgamesh XI and an essential parallel for Genesis 1–9. The edition by Lambert and Millard (1969) was decisive, because it brought together the complete sequence for the first time: creation, crisis and flood. In the poem, 'Anunnaki' and 'Igigi' designate, respectively, the gods who rule and those who labor. It does not describe any colony of beings from elsewhere; it is a theology of the human condition.
c.entradas.atrahasis.detalles.0: Ipiq-Aya's colophon divides the work into three tablets, about 1,200 lines in all.
c.entradas.atrahasis.detalles.1: The god slain to create humans is called We-ila (or Aw-ila, depending on the reading). His blood is mixed with clay.
c.entradas.atrahasis.detalles.2: The mother goddess Nintu/Mami shapes the first seven men and seven women.
c.entradas.atrahasis.detalles.3: Before the flood, Enlil sends an epidemic, a drought and a famine.
c.entradas.atrahasis.detalles.4: Enki warns Atrahasis by speaking to a reed wall, so as not to break his oath of secrecy.
c.entradas.atrahasis.fuentes_primarias.0: Old Babylonian tablets from Sippar (Ipiq-Aya's copy), British Museum
c.entradas.atrahasis.fuentes_primarias.1: Neo-Assyrian fragments from the Library of Ashurbanipal, Nineveh
c.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.nombre_origi: Ziusudra (Sumerian, 'life of prolonged days'); ETCSL 1.7.4; called the 'Eridu Genesis' by Jacobsen
c.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.fecha_texto: A single, badly damaged tablet from Nippur, c. 1600 BC (late Old Babylonian). There is a bilingual fragment from the 7th century BC.
c.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.resumen: The gods decide to destroy humankind with a flood. Ziusudra, king of Shuruppak, receives a warning and builds a great boat. After seven days and seven nights of storm he offers a sacrifice to Utu, and An and Enlil grant him eternal life in Dilmun.
c.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.interpretaci:
It is the oldest known Sumerian version of the Mesopotamian flood. More than a third of the text has been lost. Jacobsen reconstructed an 'Eridu Genesis' that also included the creation of humans and the first cities, but that reconstruction is hypothetical. The Sumerian King List also places the flood between the 'antediluvian' kings and the later ones, and some versions name Ziusudra.

Assyriologists see it as part of a tradition running parallel to Atrahasis and Gilgamesh XI: Ziusudra, Atrahasis and Utnapishtim are the same character under different names. Attempts have been made to link it to flood layers at Ur, Shuruppak or Kish, but those layers do not coincide in time. A connection with any specific flood remains unproven.
c.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.detalles.0: Tablet CBS 10673 in the Penn Museum, published by Arno Poebel in 1914.
c.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.detalles.1: Ziusudra is king and priest of Shuruppak.
c.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.detalles.2: The flood lasts seven days and seven nights.
c.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.detalles.3: In the end, Ziusudra receives immortality and settles in Dilmun, 'where the sun rises'.
c.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.fuentes_prim: Bilingual fragment from the Library of Ashurbanipal
